context: A box contains purple, orange, white and pink coloured blocks, and one block is selected at random.

params.why: the correct fraction is already in simplest form, and so are the two distractors built from it, so no option is given away by being reducible
the part-to-rest distractor and the opposite-event distractor must be different values

stem: A box contains coloured blocks: {=a} purple, {=b} orange, {=c} white and {=d} pink. A block is selected at random. Which of the following is the probability that the block is purple?
solution: First we work out how many blocks there are in total. This gives us the sample space: $n(S)={=a}+{=b}+{=c}+{=d}={=tot}$ .
The event is that the block is purple. There are ${=a}$ purple blocks, so $n(E)={=a}$ .
Every block is equally likely to be selected, so: $\begin{aligned}P(\text{purple})&=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}\\&=\frac{{=a}}{{=tot}}\end{aligned}$ This fraction is already in simplest form.

The four colours are not equally likely, because there are different numbers of blocks of each colour, so the answer is not $\frac{1}{4}$ . The total ${=tot}$ counts all the blocks, not only the ones that are not purple, and the numerator counts the purple blocks, not the others.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Divides by the outcomes outside the event
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student writes n(E) over the number of outcomes that are not in the event (a part-to-rest comparison) instead of over n(S), the total number of outcomes in the sample space.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Counts the outcomes that are not in the event
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student counts the outcomes that are not in the event instead of the ones that are, so n(E) is the wrong set, and writes that count over n(S).

notes: Standard-tier diagnostic multiple choice on book ex14-8-11a (coloured blocks). It gives the catalogued misconception unequal-outcomes-counted-as-equal a home (the 1/4 option: four colours, so one in four) and declares two further named errors of n(E)/n(S). Constraint gcd(a, tot) = 1 makes the correct fraction irreducible, and gcd(a, tot - a) = gcd(tot - a, tot) = gcd(a, tot) = 1 makes both built distractors irreducible too, so reducibility never identifies the correct option. The four values are always distinct (1/4 is excluded by a >= 12 with gcd 1, and the last require separates the two built distractors). The stem carries the variation, so distinct_by_choices is not set. Verified offline: about 59% of random draws are accepted, 11000+ distinct instances.
